messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Psychiatrist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 47

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Media / News: Related news, Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Redirection: I think of something else
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 62, Rafael Ortega had spent most of his adult life becoming the kind of psychiatrist other people trusted with unbearable stories. He was a single man who had built a careful life in the United States after leaving Latin America decades earlier, and for years he had kept his own history largely sealed off. In his twenties he had been detained and tortured by state authorities. What stayed with him most sharply were not a tidy sequence of events but fragments that still arrived with brutal force: the sound of men speaking around him in rapid, overlapping voices he could not make out, the presence of uniforms in doorways and corridors, the sickening certainty that the people holding him could do anything they wanted because no one would stop them. Some stretches of that period remained completely blank to him, while other moments were preserved with terrible precision.

In the years after he immigrated, Rafael had tried to make himself into someone defined by competence and usefulness rather than by what had been done to him. He entered medicine, became a psychiatrist, and learned how to move through hospitals and clinics with a calm, measured authority. Yet the setting of his work also carried quiet dangers. A television in a hospital waiting room playing international news, a police officer escorting an agitated patient through the emergency department, or a burst of incomprehensible chatter in a crowded hallway could strike him with no warning. In those moments the memory did not feel like remembering. It arrived as a full sensory reliving, completely real across sight, sound, and bodily feeling, as if time had dropped away and he were back in detention. Because the memory could be triggered instantly by his surroundings, he had come to scan the world for exactly those cues.

As these episodes accumulated, Rafael grew more certain that the old injury had never truly ended. News stories about political violence or state abuses did not simply upset him; they confirmed what he already believed, that institutions meant to protect ordinary people had failed, just as they had failed him. Seeing men in uniform or hearing official language on television brought up not only fear but bitterness that those responsible had never been held to account. He spoke with increasing conviction about having lost his connection to his community and culture. The country he had left no longer felt like his, but neither did the life he had built in America fully repair that rupture. Those meanings sharpened the sting of his triggers: uniforms were not just uniforms, news was not just news, and confused voices were not just background noise. They carried the whole weight of betrayal.

Once the reliving began to return more often, Rafael started organizing his life around not setting it off. He avoided going out unless he had to, especially to places where there might be crowds, police presence, or televisions showing current events. Before nearly any interaction, even routine exchanges, he found himself rehearsing what he would say. He told himself this was simply preparation, but he knew it was also an effort to prevent the disorientation he felt when rapid or unclear speech around him made his body go rigid. When intrusive recollections broke through, he would force his mind onto something else immediately, redirecting himself with professional tasks, mental lists, or deliberately unrelated topics. These habits gave him brief relief, but they also kept the memory poised and unchanged, ready to return in the same total form the next time a cue slipped past him.

Over months and years, the avoidance narrowed his world. Outside of work he spent more time alone in his apartment, limiting invitations and stepping back from social and cultural spaces that once might have anchored him. That retreat deepened his sense that he had lost his community, and the loss in turn made every fresh reminder feel like proof that he had been abandoned by both his country and history. Even at work, where he remained highly skilled, the cycle intruded. If he heard garbled voices through a clinic door, he would tense before entering; if a patient encounter involved security staff, he could feel himself already bracing for the memory. The more he rehearsed and redirected, the more alert he became to danger signals in his surroundings, and the more quickly those signals could pull him back into the sensory force of the torture.

He finally sought help after realizing that the effort required to keep himself composed was beginning to erode the life he had built. He had recently left a staff meeting early after a news clip playing nearby and the sight of a uniformed officer in the corridor brought on such a vivid reliving that he had to lock himself in his office until it passed. What frightened Rafael most was not only the intensity of the memories, but the possibility that he would continue disappearing from his own life—cut off from colleagues, from culture, from ordinary freedom—while the men and institutions he believed had destroyed so much remained untouched. What he hoped for, cautiously, was not to forget, but to stop living as though the cell door were still open somewhere just behind him.
